I also put $7,200 into a used minivan because our old car kept dying and Mia still has monthly follow-ups — though honestly it's our everyday car too now. That leaves about $20,100, which I'm holding for Mia's future needs and our family's stability. When a donor named Hal — he gave $2,500 — asked on the page about the leftover, I posted the full itemized breakdown; I've hidden nothing. Now I hear he's messaging other donors saying I'm "pocketing sick-kid money." The platform's own terms say the organizer decides what happens to surplus. After everything we've been through, is the leftover ours to keep?

Two and a half years ago a man in my congregation, Victor, talked me into putting $20,000 of my retirement savings into his home-repair business — he promised $24,000 back over three years, "better than your CD," and showed me revenue numbers he later admitted he'd inflated by about forty percent. The business failed a year and a half in; the local downturn was real, but so were the fake numbers. I'll grant him this: he came and confessed the inflation himself before I'd ever have found it, apologized to me privately, and told the elders. He's paid back $6,200 over two years — he makes about $52,000 with a family of four — so I'm still out $13,800, and my roof needs replacing, a $14,000 job. I want the money back within twelve months, and I think he should stand up and tell the congregation what he did, since he found me through church. He's offering $300 a month, which is almost four more years. We've both asked Elder Raymond to mediate and he'll propose terms Sunday. What should I hold out for?

I'm a solo tile installer and I retiled the entry floor and front-counter area of a small hardware store. There was one real problem: about 15 tiles near the entry settled with a slight lippage — uneven edges, a little trip-lip — my mistake, and I ground them down and re-set them within two days of her telling me, no charge. It cost me maybe $90 in materials and my time; nobody got hurt and she didn't lose any business over it. I also did three extra rounds of touch-ups she asked for — a grout-color rematch, a threshold strip, a re-caulk — past the two in the contract, and never billed her. Now the owner, Colette, is five weeks late on the final $1,200 and says the lippage "made the shop look sloppy" and she wants $400 off. I need that money. Do I have to take the cut?

Part of this is to honor my late father, who used that pantry decades ago and would've loved to see it. But honestly I've also felt taken for granted after all these years. The development person seems hesitant about the "above the other donors" part. Am I being unreasonable, and how do I get what I asked for?
